I tried blink because I was having paste issues with one or two competing products. It might seem clever to avoid traditional GUI controls in favor of keyboard shortcuts, but it doesn’t work in practice. I’m in the middle of production server support, and I’ve already spent too much time trying to figure out how to make this product work. It’s bad enough to charge a recurring yearly fee for a shell application based on GPL code, but to make an unusable product in the process is a step too far. Uninstalling and requesting a refund.

title: Bad upgrade path—buyer beware

I’m all for developers moving to a subscription model to support their business, or charging for a new version, but closing the upgrade path completely is a scummy business practice and it’s part of why this business model is reviled. Other Mac and iPad tools that have migrated to this model have a support line for migrating if you missed the advertised window. Alfred, another power user tool on MacOS, is a good example of how to handle upgrades without screwing over your users.

title: Frustrating. Needs error handling.
body: The SSH functionality works fine. The aliases are great. I do wish they also auto-completed for ssh-copy-id to make setup easier but that shouldn’t be an issue long term. My issue was with VSCode integration and the complete lack of error reporting if you don’t format your remote path correctly. For reference for anyone about to refund the app like I was, these did not work: code <remote>:~ code <remote>:~/ code <remote>:~/folder But this DID work: code <remote>:~/folder/ There is no error message that the path was bad or that opening the remote failed. It just completely ignored the argument and behaved like you’d only typed “code”. I also couldn’t find any UI to save or re-open recent remotes so you must use the terminal commands. I’m glad it works but its nuts that it behaves like this. Hope this helps someone, this detail was not in the docs.

title: Another iTunes app goes from buying (owning) it to subscription - No thank you!
body: I purchased the original version of Blink for $19.95 back when it was a “non-subscription” based type of selling model, i.e., you pay for the software 1x and you “own it.” Now the author of this iTunes app has decided to change his iTunes selling business model to an annual $19.95 subscription based model. Yes, the original Blink version purchasers do get access to the newer Blink version, but not the advanced $19.95 per year version. Back when we purchased the original version of the software, it was NOT based on a subscription based type of model, but the author has now decided to move to a annual cash cow model after the fact. The original Blink app purchasers who purchased the app thinking they “owned it” and any updates for it for life, is now over and to get the advanced feature sets the original Blink purchasers must pay annually for their original version of Blink is no longer being updated, only the subscription based model of Blink. I consider this to be akin to a bait and switch type of selling approach. If you really want to take care of your original Blink purchasers, then grandfather them into the $19.95 newer version of Blink subscription model for free for life - - not switching from what we originally purchased Blink for (lifetime 1x purchase) to a subscription based model that even the original Blink non-subscription based purchasers are now forced to go to and pay annually for to get all the future feature sets / updates. My point is, if you want to sell a subscription based model, then START FROM THE GET GO with that subscription based model so that users like me, whom purchase a non-subscription based app from you thinking we’ll get all future updates / feature sets and then switch business models on us from a “own for life” that we originally purchased the app as, to a annual subscription model that charges even original purchasers of your non-subscription model over to. I simply hate it when app developers offer their apps on the iTunes Store as a non-subscription model and then decide that they can make more $$$ after the fact and force original non-subscription purchasers to download the newer subscription app and stop further development of the original non-subscription based app they originally purchased. It consider this to be more than a bit unethical.

title: I hate that this app is good.
body: I have been on a months-long quest to find an acceptable terminal app that I can actually own instead of rent. Unfortunately, every other option I tried (Termius was second-best) has dealbreaking flaws of one kind or another. Blink does not. It has flaws, but no dealbreakers. It also has several excellent and very useful day-to-day features that no other terminal app I have tried manages to implement all at once, and a few really good UI ideas I've never seen in a mobile terminal before. It's *relatively* stable for a mobile terminal app, the screen drawing issues aren't *usually* bad enough to force me to close the app and start over—a low bar, but no other app consistently meets it. And it feels and works remarkably like a NORMAL TERMINAL instead of somebody's fever dream of what the Terminal of the Future should be. The business model disgusts me. The *instant* I hear of an acceptable mobile terminal with an ethical business model, I will switch. I really hope I can do that before I need to pay next year's terminal rent. Two stars.

title: Free version nag-screens are a real thing
body: I like the app and what it does. And I don’t really have a problem with a yearly subscription of $20 for the full version, I am not against subscriptions per se. I am also ok with the free version being limited in some way (including by a nag-screen) - that is after all how you evaluate before purchasing. But I have to say, the way that the developers have implemented the nag-screen to upgrade is a first for me. So much so that this is the first review I have ever made in the AppStore and this nag-screen implementation has turned me off the app so much that I will not be subscribing. This may not be a problem for everyone. But saying “there is a nag-screen, no big deal” does not give the full picture. They are transparent that the nag-screen will come up “up to a max of 3x per day”. What they don’t say is that there is a timer on the nag-screen that interrupts what you are doing for a significant time: 20seconds perhaps? Worse, if you “shake your device to fill this up quicker” the timer is supposed to be shorter but there really is not way to tell if that is so. As long as it counts down clearly, 5 seconds I could live with. Maybe even 10. But the timer as it is is just too random and long - and being asked to “shake to fill” is just juvenile… If the developers do not want to limit the app in other ways (only offer a subset of features?) my suggestion is to change that timeout to allow a limited “give me 5min” holds before it is forced (I would not be happy if I had a time critical situation and being forced to pause for 20sec). And rather than a “shake” prompt, my $0.02 is to just change it into a “take a break, it is better for you anyway” count down the seconds message…

title: Subscriptions are an unsustainable leech to consumers. App is good.
body: I’ll preface this review by saying I hate subscriptions. I will never rent software. The bulk of this review concerns the new subscription model, so feel free to skip it if your feelings differ. I saw a developer response to a review indicate that the new subscription model exists to pay for new features that incur a server cost. That’s fine and understandable. However, requiring all users to pay these fees even if they have no intention of using these new features is pretty gross. Ideally you would only pay the rental fee if you were actually using the service. It’s nice that they allow existing users to continue using the base application nag free. I’ll give a star for that. The application itself is good. If I weren’t grandfathered in, however, I would look elsewhere. It’s not sustainable as an average consumer to rent every piece of software we use in perpetuity.

title: Only a wrap of Web VSCode

So it is, of course, unable to install any code completion plugin in VSCode, no C++, no Python and even no JavaScipt. As a result, the VSCode is just a partially-functioning editor with a good theme. That’s something at least

title: REDACT
body: Ah, the description to migrate from classic to this updated version is a bit obscure. Fortunately, I found it and moshed again. It works fine. Thank you. body: It would be nice to have a way to highlight and copy a long prompt, rather than pinch to zoom out.

title: Most visually appealing, minimal SSH/Mosh client (minus the subscription model)
body: This app is my favorite SSH and Mosh client. I appreciate the local Unix utilities it provides and the fact that it looks and behaves like a terminal emulator. The visual minimalism by default is excellent. My one issue is with the recurring subscription model. I would rate it five stars if there was a one-time purchase option (even if it was per device — I’d happily pay $5-10 per device I needed Blink on). It makes it hard to recommend to interested friends or colleagues when there isn’t a free option or a one-time purchase option. Thankfully, I was grandfathered into the Blink Legacy pricing (which offered a one-time purchase). Please bring one-time purchases back!

title: Excellent remote shell and terminal networking tools
body: This is the best ssh, terminal, ping, etc tools set I’ve used on iPad. Easy to use. Full features for everything I need to log in to my home machines (I connect via tailscale) and work remotely. It has saved me many times already when VNC has gone wonky or the network is too slow.

title: My terminal

title: Either love it or hate it? I loved it.
body: Based on the ratings, it seems that users either love or hate it. I am pleased with it, as it allows me to remotely open a terminal that is connected to my remote MacBook Pro. A terminal is not an interface for the faint-of-heart, but for more technically oriented users. It required some work on my MacBook Pro, though it was a breeze as ClaudeCode held my hand throughout the process. With this app now I can open a ClaudeCode terminal in my iPhone, or iPad, via SSH or MOSH, and work on it as if I was directly sitting in front my Mac. Worth $20/year in my opinion. Again: it requires some work on the Mac side. Based on the few reviews I read, seems to me, that those complaining either did not know how to set up the Mac side correctly, and/or do not want to pay for it. I have TailScale on my Mac, which made it easier though.

title: John

title: Simply Amazing for a Developer
body: I’m running a software startup on top of a full time job. I’ve used every terminal under the sun for MacOS and this is truly the only one I feel at home on. It just works the way I the way I expect and love that it has it’s own shell that you use to connect or send commands. I love how mosh keeps things connected. When I go on lunch breaks or can get away from my day job for a few minutes I use my iPad via cellular/tailscale and have no hiccups. Being able to grab a lightweight device and complete 95% of what I can do with a MBP by connecting to my MBP is just amazing. The VSCode integration works well too however using neovim/tmux on the MacBook via Mosh is my preferred flow. The MacBook has to stay connected to peripherals required to validate my code changes and now I can work remote and don’t have to splurge on a higher end Mac mini or studio or carry a ton of stuff with me:)

title: Hands Down The Best iPhone Shell
body: Disregard the low review score, which are from a pricing model change a couple years back. This shell looks and works great, comes with mosh, ssh, netcat, ping, etc, ssh keys and user profiles, tabs / windows and a special command key (ie, cmd + t to open a new tab, cmd + w to close a tab, etc). My only complaint is accessing the configuration requires running a command in the shell. Use tmux with mosh and a VPN and you can code from anywhere.

Cons: there is a bug with the cmd-w shortcut remapping, but someone else posted a solution on Github luckily.

title: Amazing app
body: I use Blink every day. The developers are extremely responsive and have fixed many issues so that Blink works great with Stage Manager on an external display. Blink allows me to be productive on the iPad, a device that increasingly misses the mark on functionality for pro users while simultaneously being more complicated for average users. While I don't personally have the need for Blink Build, nor do I use Blink Code, I'm happy to support a team that makes such a great app. If you are frustrated by the pricing changes I encourage you to pause a moment and reflect on how to encourage great apps like this to be created and maintained outside of a few large corporations. Consider supporting iPad app sustainability for small teams.

body: It just works. Does everything I need it to do and keeps out of the way. I never have to think about the app while working on my servers. The Files.app integration is icing on the cake!

title: Immediate love
body: I’m not one to write reviews but this just blew me out of the water. Perfectly simple and yet remarkably complex. It presents itself as a simple shell (which it is), opening to a lone “blink>” prompt with no clear way to interact with it, but the configuration screen is just a ‘config’ away. It kind of reminds me a bit of ConnectBot if it ran through a Termux interface (Android concert here) and that is high praise in my mind. I rifled through hordes of other apps that had nothing but problems. Most of them were doing too much, charging too much, and not being open source at all. Bah. That said there is but one thing I am not a fan of: VS Code. Don’t get me wrong: no choice for code editor is going to make everyone happy (I’m one of the few that would be content with plain old vi). That is the point though: perhaps integration with external editors would make more sense. It’s nit picky, though. That degree of integration is nice, having a full fledged editor is fantastic, and being able to work offline is a major bonus. Keep up the fantastic work!

Within seconds I was able to connect to my target device, and understand the interface Blink provides. Well done.

title: Turns my iPad into a full Linux terminal
body: I've been using Blink for several years and it just keeps getting better and better. I consider it an absolutely essential app for my iPad Pro, where I use it to SSH into a Linux machine to have full access to Emacs. And using Mosh (instead of SSH directly) means that I can simply open my iPad at any time and my previous SSH session is still there, immediately ready for me to use. Amazing. The app developer(s) are highly responsive and take feedback seriously and their dedication to keeping the software open-source makes me more than happy to support this app. I'm not a fan of subscriptions, but I was more than happy to subscribe to help support future development. I'd give it 10 stars if I could.

title: subscription and no longer open source?
body: Blink 14 user here, got all old features for free. Code is not there, assume it’s in the Plus plan. But why subscription for a shell app though? And the new Blink shell seems no longer Open Source. Edit: dev responded. It’s still OSS and Code is available for free.

title: Great app keeps getting better
body: I’ve been using Blink for a few years now on two different iPads. The price is well worth it for many reasons. Top reasons are things like turning on geo tracking to keep your ssh sessions active where you can’t use mosh, great ssh key management, and super-fast rendering of the terminals. There are others, but this is a good start. The v15 update is really great. Adding in VSCode integration is wicked cool, and works really well. To top it all off, the support from the developer is top-notch. I had an issue, submitted a github issue, and had a response within minutes (it was user error…). And just scouring the GitHub issue tracker, and seeing the activity from the development crew, is very reassuring. Bottom line: I’ve tried a few different terminal apps with decent success. Once I purchased Blink, I uninstalled the other ones. It does everything I want, does it well, and probably does more than I use. Great app, great support.
